landmarks.name: Victoria Falls
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest and most famous waterfalls in the world, located on the Zambezi River at the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe.

wiki.extract: Victoria Falls is a waterfall on the Zambezi River, located on the border between Zambia and Zimbabwe. It is one of the world's largest waterfalls, with a width of 1,708 m (5,604 ft). The region around it has a high degree of biodiversity in both plants and animals.

landmarks.name: South Luangwa National Park
landmarks.writeup: A renowned wildlife sanctuary known for its walking safaris and diverse animal populations including elephants, lions, and hippos.

wiki.extract:
South Luangwa National Park is a national park in eastern Zambia that was founded as a game reserve in 1938 and became a national park in 1972. It covers 9,050 km2 (3,490 sq mi) in the valley of the Luangwa River, which forms its eastern boundary in the Eastern Province of Zambia. It is bordered to the west by a steep escarpment, the Muchinga Escarpment in Muchinga and Central Provinces. The Luangwa Valley lies at the end of the East African Rift valley.
The meandering Luangwa River and its lagoons support over 400 bird species and more than 60 mammal species including Rhodesian giraffe, African bush elephant and African buffalo.

landmarks.name: Lower Zambezi National Park
landmarks.writeup: A protected area along the Zambezi River offering opportunities for canoeing, fishing, and wildlife viewing.

wiki.extract: The Lower Zambezi National Park lies on the north bank of the Zambezi River in southeastern Zambia. Until 1983 when the area was declared a national park, the area was the private game reserve of Zambia's president. This meant that the park was protected from mass tourism and now remains one of the few untouched wilderness areas left in Africa. On the opposite bank is Zimbabwe's Mana Pools National Park. The two parks sit on the Zambezi floodplain ringed by mountains.

landmarks.name: Kafue National Park
landmarks.writeup: One of Africa's largest national parks, home to a wide variety of wildlife and diverse ecosystems.

wiki.extract: Kafue National Park is the largest national park in Zambia, covering an area of about 22,400 km2 (8,600 sq mi). It is the second largest national park in Africa and home to 152 mammal species. There are also 515 bird species, 70 reptile species, 58 species of fish and 36 amphibious species.

cultural_events.name: Kuomboka Ceremony
cultural_events.writeup: An annual traditional ceremony of the Lozi people marking the movement of the king from the flooded plains to higher ground.

wiki.extract:
Kuomboka is a word in the Lozi language; it literally means 'to get out of water'. In today's Zambia it is applied to a traditional ceremony that takes place at the end of the rain season, when the upper Zambezi River floods the plains of the Western Province.
The festival celebrates the move of the Litunga, king of the Lozi people, from his compound at Lealui in the Barotse Floodplain of the Zambezi River to Limulunga on higher ground. The return trip is usually held in August with a less publicized journey called the Kufuluhela.

cultural_events.name: Nc'wala Ceremony
cultural_events.writeup: A celebration by the Ngoni people to mark the first fruits harvest and honor their ancestors.

wiki.extract: Chipata is a city and administrative centre of the Eastern Province of Zambia and Chipata District. It was declared the 5th city of the country, after Lusaka, Ndola, Kitwe and Livingstone, by President Edgar Lungu on 24 February 2017. The city has undergone rapid economic and infrastructure growth in the years, leading up to city status.

food_writeup: Zambian cuisine features staple foods such as nshima (a maize-based porridge), often served with vegetables, beans, and meats like fish or beef. Traditional dishes emphasize locally sourced ingredients and communal eating.
brief_history: Zambia gained independence from British colonial rule in 1964. It was formerly known as Northern Rhodesia. The country has a history of copper mining and has experienced periods of economic growth and challenges since independence.

commentary.inflation_management: Zambia's inflation tracks copper and the kwacha. It was contained at 6-9% from 2010 to 2015, then the 2015 copper crash and kwacha collapse sent it to 17.9% in 2016. Tighter policy brought it down to 6.6% by 2017, but the 2020 default and currency crisis pushed it to 22.0% in 2021, the series high. The Hichilema government's tightening and IMF anchor stabilized it: 11.0% in 2022, 10.9% in 2023, then drought and currency pressure lifted it to 15.0% in 2024 and a projected 13.9% in 2025. The Bank of Zambia has no formal inflation target but has acted as one, hiking aggressively through the crisis.
commentary.debt_management: Zambia's debt is the textbook commodity boom-bust: from 18.9% of GDP in 2010, the series low (post-HIPC/MDRI), the Patriotic Front government borrowed heavily, including $3 billion in Eurobonds and large Chinese loans, driving the ratio to 140.0% in 2020, the series high. In November 2020 Zambia became Africa's first COVID-era sovereign defaulter. The August 2021 election of Hakainde Hichilema unlocked a $1.3 billion IMF program (approved August 31, 2022) and a G20 Common Framework restructuring: debt fell to a projected 86.0% in 2025. The restructuring's slow progress, held up by creditor disputes, showed the new architecture's flaws, but Zambia is the proof that it can eventually work.

key_events.event: Copper boom; HIPC-era low debt (18.9% of GDP); Eurobond borrowing spree began.
Copper crash and kwacha collapse; inflation hit 17.9%; debt surged past 60%.
November 2020: missed Eurobond payment, becoming Africa's first pandemic-era sovereign defaulter; debt hit 140% of GDP.
Hakainde Hichilema won the presidency (August 2021), promising economic repair.
August 31, 2022: IMF approved a $1.3 billion program; Common Framework restructuring began.
Severe drought (2024) hit agriculture and hydropower; debt restructuring neared completion.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued IMF-anchored recovery: debt declining from 86% of GDP, inflation easing toward single digits, and copper revenues supporting the kwacha. Upside comes from the energy transition's copper demand and completed restructuring; downside is copper prices or a return to the borrowing habits that caused the crisis. Uncertainty is moderate: Zambia has the framework right, but the test is whether discipline survives the next election and the next copper boom.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
